mainTopic: Why רבי מאיר is strict about a doubtful עירוב: are תחומין Torah law, and how does this fit his other rulings on doubt?
overview: This amud continues the משנה about an עירוב תחומין that may have become unusable before or after nightfall on ערב שבת. In that doubt רבי מאיר is strict and רבי יוסי is lenient. First the גמרא explains that the burnt case shows how far רבי יוסי's leniency goes, and the impure תרומה case shows how far רבי מאיר's strictness goes. Then it asks why רבי מאיר is strict at all, since a משנה about doubtful immersion is lenient for rabbinic impurity. The answer is that רבי מאיר holds תחומין are a Torah law. The גמרא challenges this from רבי מאיר's ruling that we 'pierce mountains' when measuring. It answers that this leniency was his teacher's view, which he only reported ('I have heard'). Next the גמרא contrasts this with רבי מאיר's leniency about a person touched at night and found dead in the morning, which is also a Torah-level doubt. רבי ירמיה answers that a שרץ sat on the עירוב all through בין השמשות, but that does not fit רבי יוסי's ruling. So רבה and רב יוסף explain that the doubt comes from two sets of witnesses who contradict each other.

steps.title: Each example shows the full strength of one opinion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its answer: the burnt עירוב case shows how strong רבי יוסי's leniency is, and the impure תרומה case shows how strong רבי מאיר's stringency is.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The משנה taught the case of a burnt עירוב] to show you the strength of רבי יוסי's position. It taught the case of תרומה that became impure to show you the strength of רבי מאיר's position.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is completing its answer to why the משנה gave two separate examples of an עירוב that became unusable. Each example teaches how far one side of the argument goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the burnt case the עירוב no longer exists at all, yet רבי יוסי is still lenient about the doubt. That is a strong leniency. In the תרומה case the food is still physically there and only its status changed, yet רבי מאיר is still stringent. That is a strong stringency.

keyTerms.meaning: To show you his strength, meaning how far his opinion goes
[The משנה] taught
The portion of produce given to a כהן; it is forbidden to eat once impure
And it became ritually impure

steps.confusionAlert: The opening words 'תנא נשרף' belong to earlier. This step begins in the middle of that sentence, so read it as the ending of an answer already in progress.

phrases.english: to show you the strength of Rabbi Yosei's position.
phrases.notes: Continues 'תנא נשרף' earlier. He is lenient even though the עירוב is completely gone.

phrases.english: It taught the case of terumah that became impure
to show you the strength of Rabbi Meir's position.
phrases.notes: He is stringent even though the food is still physically present.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer earlier about why the משנה lists two cases.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why did the משנה need both the burnt case and the impure תרומה case?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each case shows the furthest reach of a different opinion: the burnt case for רבי יוסי and the תרומה case for רבי מאיר.

steps.title: Does רבי מאיר really rule stringently in a doubt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether רבי מאיר really holds that a doubt must be treated stringently.
steps.simpleTranslation: And does רבי מאיר really hold that a doubt is treated stringently?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a challenge against רבי מאיר's ruling in our משנה. This line opens the attack, and the next steps bring the source behind it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In our משנה רבי מאיר treats a doubtful עירוב strictly. The question implies that elsewhere רבי מאיר is lenient in a similar kind of doubt. The גמרא is about to show where.

keyTerms.meaning: And does he hold?
A doubt is treated stringently

phrases.english: And does Rabbi Meir hold that a doubt is treated stringently?
phrases.notes: The question is rhetorical; it signals a challenge.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining the משנה's wording to challenging רבי מאיר's ruling itself.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's stringent ruling about a doubtful עירוב in our משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Elsewhere רבי מאיר seems to be lenient about a doubt in a rabbinic matter, and עירוב is also rabbinic.

steps.title: The מקוה case: in doubt, he stays impure
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה about doubts in טבילה. In each listed doubt, the person remains impure.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in a משנה: An impure person went down to immerse. It is unclear whether he immersed or not. Or, even if he did immerse, it is unclear whether the מקוה had forty סאה. Or, there were two מקואות, one with forty סאה and one without, and he immersed in one of them but does not know which. In each of these doubts, he is impure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins quoting the source it will use against רבי מאיר. This first part lists three kinds of doubt about immersion, and in all of them the person stays impure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three levels of doubt: whether he immersed at all, whether the מקוה was big enough, and which of two מקואות he used. In each one he keeps his original impure status. This part alone does not yet contradict רבי מאיר; the contradiction comes in the lenient half of the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't we learn in a משנה?
To immerse in a מקוה
Forty סאה, the minimum amount of water for a valid מקוה
Ritual baths
In his doubt, he is impure

steps.confusionAlert: This impure ruling is not the part that contradicts רבי מאיר. The challenge comes from the next lines, where the person in doubt is ruled pure.

phrases.english: But didn't we learn: an impure person who went down to immerse,
and it is unclear whether he immersed or did not immerse;

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲפִילּוּ טָבַל — סָפֵק טָבַל בְּאַרְבָּעִים סְאָה,
phrases.english: and even if he did immerse, it is unclear whether he immersed in forty se'ah
or did not immerse in forty se'ah;
and similarly, two ritual baths:
one has forty se'ah in it,
and one does not have forty se'ah in it;
and he immersed in one of them,
but he does not know in which of them he immersed:
in his doubt, he is impure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins quoting the משנה that supports the challenge raised in step 2.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that רבי מאיר is not always stringent in a doubt.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A משנה about doubtful immersion (משנה מקואות).

steps.title: This applies only to severe impurity
steps.stepSummary: The quoted משנה limits its impure ruling to טומאה חמורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: When is this said? With severe impurity.
steps.whatsHappening: The quoted משנה limits the rule just stated. Ruling the person impure applies only to severe impurity, and this line sets up the contrast that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: טומאה חמורה means impurity from the Torah, which comes from a primary source of impurity. Because that impurity is serious, a doubt about whether it was removed leaves the person impure.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case are these words said?
Severe impurity, from the Torah

phrases.english: In what case are these words said?
With severe impurity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the impure ruling of step 3 to severe impurity.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A doubt about immersion leaves a person impure only when the impurity is severe.

steps.title: With light rabbinic impurity, in doubt he is pure
steps.stepSummary: For light, rabbinic impurity, the same three doubts about immersion leave the person pure. This is the source that challenges רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But with light impurity, the outcome is different. Examples: he ate impure foods or drank impure liquids, or he put his head and most of his body into drawn water, or three לוגין of drawn water fell on his head and most of his body. If he then went down to immerse, and there is a doubt whether he immersed, or whether the water was forty סאה, or which of two מקואות he used, then in his doubt he is pure.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the punchline of the quoted משנה. For impurity that is only rabbinic, the person is pure when there is a doubt. That is a lenient ruling on a doubt, which is the opposite of what רבי מאיר says about the עירוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating impure food, drinking impure liquids, and contact with drawn water (מים שאובין) cause impurity only by rabbinic decree. In a doubt about such impurity, the ruling is lenient. Since עירוב is also a rabbinic institution, the גמרא is building the challenge: why would רבי מאיר be strict about a doubtful עירוב? The challenge assumes this unnamed ruling is רבי מאיר's view. The next step shows why: רבי יוסי is named as the dissenter, and an unnamed משנה usually follows רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: Light impurity, imposed only by rabbinic decree
Drawn water, carried in a vessel, as opposed to spring water or rainwater
His head and most of his body
Three לוגין, a liquid measure
In his doubt, he is pure

steps.whatToRemember: The quoted משנה is strict about a doubt in Torah impurity and lenient about a doubt in rabbinic impurity. That leniency appears to clash with רבי מאיר's strict ruling about a doubtful עירוב.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the principle that a doubt in a rabbinic matter (ספק דרבנן) is treated leniently. That principle is the basis of the contradiction the גמרא must now resolve.

phrases.english: But with light impurity,
for example, one who ate impure foods
or drank impure liquids,
or one who put his head and most of his body into drawn water,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁנָּפְלוּ עַל רֹאשׁוֹ וְעַל רוּבּוֹ
phrases.english: or on whose head and most of his body there fell
three log of drawn water,
and he went down to immerse;
and it is unclear whether he immersed or did not immerse;

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲפִילּוּ טָבַל — סָפֵק טָבַל בְּאַרְבָּעִים סְאָה,
phrases.english: and even if he did immerse, it is unclear whether he immersed in forty se'ah
or did not immerse in forty se'ah;
and similarly, two ritual baths:
one has forty se'ah in it,
and one does not have forty se'ah in it;
and he immersed in one of them,
but he does not know in which of them he immersed:
in his doubt, he is pure.
phrases.notes: The lenient ruling that drives the challenge.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the contrast set up in step 4: light impurity, where the ruling in a doubt is lenient.
steps.raayaObject: That a doubt in a rabbinic matter is treated leniently, which contradicts רבי מאיר's strictness about the עירוב.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The second half of the משנה about doubtful immersion: ספיקו טהור in טומאה קלה.

steps.title: רבי יוסי disagrees in the quoted משנה
steps.stepSummary: The quoted משנה closes with רבי יוסי's dissent: he rules the person impure even for light impurity. This completes the challenge against רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says he is impure.
steps.whatsHappening: The quoted משנה finishes: רבי יוסי argues and says the person stays impure even in the light-impurity case. The unnamed first opinion, which is usually רבי מאיר, said he is pure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An unnamed משנה (סתם משנה) usually follows רבי מאיר. So this source shows that רבי מאיר is lenient about a doubt in rabbinic impurity. That makes it hard to understand why he is strict about a doubtful עירוב, which is also rabbinic.

keyTerms.meaning: Declares impure
An unnamed משנה; usually follows רבי מאיר
Light (rabbinic) impurity

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוסי is strict HERE, but in the עירוב case he was the lenient one. The problem the גמרא is raising is about רבי מאיר, not רבי יוסי.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei declares him impure.
phrases.notes: The final words of the quoted משנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes quoting the משנה begun in steps 3-5, which makes the implied challenge to רבי מאיר complete.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי מאיר (the unnamed opinion) is lenient about a doubt in rabbinic impurity
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about doubtful immersion, with רבי יוסי dissenting

steps.title: רבי מאיר holds that תחומין are from the Torah
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי מאיר holds תחומין are a Torah law, so a doubt about them must be treated strictly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר holds that the laws of תחומין are from the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. רבי מאיר is only lenient about rabbinic doubts, and he holds that תחומין are from the Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule: a doubt about a Torah law is treated strictly, while a doubt about a rabbinic law is treated leniently. If תחומין are from the Torah, then a doubtful עירוב is a Torah-level doubt. So רבי מאיר's strictness fits with his leniency about rabbinic impurity.

keyTerms.meaning: He holds (this view)
שבת boundaries (2000 אמה)
From the Torah

steps.whyThisMatters: This ties the argument about the עירוב to a bigger question: are תחומין a Torah law or a rabbinic law?

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir holds:
Shabbat boundaries are from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge set up by the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changes the category: the עירוב case is a Torah doubt, not a rabbinic one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The עירוב is rabbinic, so רבי מאיר should be lenient there too
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר holds תחומין are from the Torah, so he is strict

steps.title: רבי מאיר allows piercing mountains when measuring
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer. A משנה reports in רבי מאיר's name that we 'pierce mountains' when measuring תחומין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי מאיר really hold that תחומין are from the Torah? But we learned: If the measuring rope cannot 'swallow' the hill, רבי דוסתאי בר ינאי said in the name of רבי מאיר: I heard that we pierce mountains.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא doubts that רבי מאיר holds תחומין are from the Torah. It quotes a משנה where רבי מאיר allows an easy way to measure over hills.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally we measure a hill with a 50-אמה rope. If the hill is too big for that, רבי מאיר says we measure as if we drilled straight through it (מקדרין). That ignores the climb and makes the distance shorter. Such an easy method suggests רבי מאיר treats תחומין as rabbinic. The next step finishes this argument.

keyTerms.meaning: To 'swallow' it; to span it with the measuring rope
We 'pierce' mountains: measure the straight flat distance through the hill
But we learned (in a משנה)

phrases.english: And does Rabbi Meir hold that boundaries are from the Torah?!
But we learned:
If he cannot swallow it (span the hill with the rope),

phrases.aramaic: בְּזוֹ אָמַר רַבִּי דּוֹסְתַּאי בַּר יַנַּאי
phrases.english: about this, Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai said
in the name of Rabbi Meir:
I heard that we pierce mountains.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי מאיר holds תחומין are from the Torah
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי מאיר allows the easy 'piercing' measurement for תחומין, which suggests they are only rabbinic

steps.title: Piercing is never used for Torah measurements
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא completes the challenge with רב נחמן's rule: we do not pierce mountains for ערי מקלט or עגלה ערופה, because those are Torah laws.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think תחומין are from the Torah, would we pierce mountains? But רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: We do not pierce mountains for cities of refuge, nor for the עגלה ערופה, because those are Torah laws.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings proof that 'piercing mountains' is only allowed for rabbinic measurements. That makes the challenge to רבי מאיר strong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן says that for Torah-law measurements, we must measure the real distance over the ground. Examples are the distance to a city of refuge and which city is closest to a dead body. Since רבי מאיר allows piercing for תחומין, it seems תחומין must be rabbinic for him. If so, the answer in step 7 falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it should enter your mind
Cities of refuge for someone who killed by accident
The calf whose neck is broken, done by the city closest to an unsolved murder
From the Torah

steps.whyThisMatters: Its strictness shows that the measuring method depends on whether a law is Torah or rabbinic. Easier methods are only for rabbinic measurements.

phrases.english: And if it should enter your mind that boundaries are from the Torah —
would we pierce (mountains)?
But Rav Nachman said
that Rabbah bar Avuh said:
We do not pierce (mountains) for cities of refuge,
nor for the calf whose neck is broken —
because they are from the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ תְּחוּמִין דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא מִי מְקַדְּרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge from step 8 by proving that piercing is only allowed for rabbinic measurements.
steps.raayaObject: That piercing mountains is not allowed for Torah-level measurements
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב נחמן in the name of רבה בר אבוה about ערי מקלט and עגלה ערופה

steps.title: The lenient ruling belongs to his teacher
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the contradiction. רבי מאיר himself holds that תחומין are Torah law. The 'piercing mountains' leniency is his teacher's opinion, which he only reported.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This view is his own, and that view is his teacher's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 8. The two statements come from two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The strict view, that תחומין are Torah law, is רבי מאיר's own opinion. The lenient 'pierce the mountains' ruling is something he passed on in his teacher's name. Since two different people said these things, there is no contradiction within רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no real contradiction
His own (opinion)
His teacher's (opinion)

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is his own, that is his teacher's.
phrases.notes: 'This' is the view that תחומין are Torah law. 'That' is the 'piercing mountains' leniency.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דִידֵיהּ, הָא דְרַבֵּיהּ
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different speakers: the two statements are split between רבי מאיר and his teacher.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both the strict and the lenient view were thought to be רבי מאיר's own, which looked like a contradiction.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the strict view, that תחומין are Torah law, is רבי מאיר's own. The leniency belongs to his teacher.

steps.title: Proof from the wording 'I have heard'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports its answer from the wording of the משנה. רבי מאיר said 'I have heard', which shows he was passing on someone else's ruling. The גמרא accepts the proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wording supports this, because it teaches: 'About this, רבי דוסתאי בר ינאי said in the name of רבי מאיר: I have heard that we pierce mountains.' Learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the משנה's own words back up the answer it just gave. It then accepts the proof with 'שמע מינה'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר did not say 'we pierce mountains' as his own ruling. He said 'I have heard', meaning he received it from a teacher. This wording fits the answer that the leniency was not his own view.

keyTerms.meaning: The wording is also precise; the text itself supports this
I have heard (I received this as a tradition)
We 'pierce' mountains: measuring as if straight through a mountain, a lenient way of measuring
Learn from it; the point is proven

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר's own view is that תחומין are Torah law. The 'pierce mountains' leniency was only something he heard from his teacher.

phrases.english: It is also precise, since it teaches:
"About this, Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai said
in the name of Rabbi Meir:
I have heard that we pierce mountains."
phrases.notes: 'I have heard' signals a tradition received from someone else.

phrases.english: Learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the תירוץ of Step 10 from the wording of the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the 'pierce mountains' leniency was רבי מאיר's teacher's view.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's phrase 'שמעתי' (I have heard) in רבי מאיר's name.

steps.title: A new contradiction in רבי מאיר's Torah-law rulings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא announces a new challenge. It will compare one Torah-law ruling of רבי מאיר with another Torah-law ruling of his.
steps.simpleTranslation: And contrast one Torah law against another Torah law, according to רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It announces a new contradiction, and the source comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We now accept that רבי מאיר treats תחומין as Torah law, which is why he is strict about a doubtful עירוב. The גמרא will now show a different Torah-law doubt where רבי מאיר is lenient. If he is lenient there, why is he strict here?

keyTerms.meaning: And contrast; set two sources against each other
A Torah-level law

phrases.english: And contrast a Torah law against a Torah law
according to Rabbi Meir,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending the idea that תחומין are Torah law, the גמרא opens a new attack built on that same idea.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's strictness about a doubtful עירוב, explained in Step 7 as Torah-level strictness.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רבי מאיר is lenient in a different Torah-level doubt, then 'Torah law' cannot be the reason he is strict here.

steps.title: Touching someone at night who was found dead
steps.stepSummary: The source for the contradiction: a person touched someone at night and found him dead in the morning. רבי מאיר rules him pure, even though corpse impurity is Torah law. The חכמים rule him impure.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: If someone touched a person at night and does not know whether he was alive or dead, and the next morning he got up and found him dead, רבי מאיר rules him pure. The חכמים rule him impure, because all impurities are judged by the time they are found.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה that shows רבי מאיר being lenient in a Torah-level doubt. This completes the contradiction announced in Step 12.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Corpse impurity is a Torah law, yet רבי מאיר is lenient. He assumes the person was still alive until we know otherwise. So why not assume the עירוב was still pure until we know it became impure? The חכמים say we judge impurity by the moment we discover it, so the person was already dead when touched.

keyTerms.meaning: Rules pure
Rule impure
As at the time they are found: we assume things were in the state we found them in

steps.confusionAlert: רבי מאיר is lenient here even though corpse impurity is a Torah law. That is exactly what makes it clash with his strictness about the עירוב.

phrases.english: As we learned: He touched someone at night,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ אִם חַי אִם מֵת,
phrases.english: and he does not know if he was alive or dead,
and the next day he got up early and found him dead.
Rabbi Meir rules him pure
and the Sages rule him impure,
because all impurities are judged as at the time they are found.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the contradiction announced in Step 12.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that רבי מאיר is lenient in Torah-level doubts.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about touching a person at night who was found dead the next morning.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה: a שרץ sat on it all of twilight
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה answers that our עירוב משנה is about a שרץ that rested on the תרומה for the entire בין השמשות. That is a different kind of doubt from the corpse case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: Our משנה is about a case where a שרץ was on it for the whole of בין השמשות.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה answers the contradiction. He explains that the עירוב case in our משנה is a special situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the corpse case, the doubt is whether the impurity existed at all when he touched. We can assume the person was alive, so רבי מאיר is lenient. In our משנה, the שרץ was definitely touching the עירוב the whole time. The only question is whether בין השמשות counts as day or night, so there is no assumption of purity to rely on, and רבי מאיר is strict.

keyTerms.meaning: A dead creeping creature that makes things impure
Twilight: the doubtful time between day and night
Our משנה (the one under discussion)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
Our mishna is where a creeping creature was on it
phrases.notes: 'It' refers to the תרומה used for the עירוב.

phrases.english: for the entire twilight period.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה: מִשְׁנָתֵנוּ שֶׁהָיָה עָלֶיהָ שֶׁרֶץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction of Steps 12–13 by narrowing the case of our משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (אוקימתא): the משנה is about a specific situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Our משנה was thought to be a simple doubt about when impurity arrived, just like the corpse case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The שרץ was on the עירוב for all of twilight. The only doubt is about the time itself, so there is no assumption of purity to lean on.

steps.title: Would רבי יוסי call this a valid doubtful עירוב?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי ירמיה. In such a case, how could רבי יוסי say 'a doubtful עירוב is valid'?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, in this case would רבי יוסי say a doubtful עירוב is valid?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי ירמיה's answer. It asks whether his version of the case still fits רבי יוסי's view in the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the same משנה, רבי יוסי says that a doubtful עירוב is valid. But if the שרץ was definitely on the עירוב for the whole of בין השמשות, the food was impure during the time the עירוב takes effect, so there is no real doubt. It is hard to believe רבי יוסי would call such an עירוב valid, so רבי ירמיה's reading seems not to fit the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if your explanation is right
A doubtful עירוב is valid (רבי יוסי's ruling)
Would he say?

phrases.english: If so,
in this case would Rabbi Yosei say
a doubtful eiruv is valid?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, בְּהָא לֵימָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי סְפֵק עֵירוּב כָּשֵׁר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case definition proposed by רבי ירמיה in Step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ירמיה's claim that the משנה is about a שרץ resting on the עירוב for all of בין השמשות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוסי rules in the same משנה that a doubtful עירוב is valid. In רבי ירמיה's case there seems to be no real doubt, so it is unlikely רבי יוסי would rule the עירוב valid.

steps.title: The doubt comes from two sets of witnesses who disagree
steps.stepSummary: רבה and רב יוסף explain that the משנה's doubtful עירוב is about two sets of witnesses. One set says the תרומה became impure before שבת. The other set says it became impure only after nightfall.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה and רב יוסף both said: Here we are dealing with two sets of witnesses. One set says the תרומה became impure while it was still day. The other set says it became impure only after nightfall.
steps.whatsHappening: Because רבי ירמיה's answer was challenged, רבה and רב יוסף give a different explanation of the case in the משנה. The doubt is about which group of witnesses to believe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עירוב only works if the food is fit to eat at בין השמשות, when שבת begins. If the תרומה became impure while it was still day, the עירוב fails. If it became impure only after nightfall, the עירוב works. Two equal sets of witnesses cancel each other out, so we cannot tell which one is right. Why this kind of doubt is different from the corpse case, so that רבי מאיר's two rulings do not contradict each other, is explained by the גמרא on the next amud (36a). It also avoids the problem raised against רבי ירמיה.

keyTerms.meaning: Both of them (both rabbis said the same thing)
Sets (groups) of witnesses
We are dealing with (this is the case under discussion)
While it was still day, before שבת began
After it became dark, after nightfall

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume this answer builds on רבי ירמיה. It replaces his picture of the case. The doubt is no longer about a שרץ resting there through בין השמשות. It is about two groups of witnesses contradicting each other.
steps.whyThisMatters: The גמרא is setting up a reason, explained on the next amud (36a), why the עירוב case and the corpse case are different kinds of doubt. A doubt caused by conflicting witnesses is not the same as a doubt caused by unknown facts.

phrases.english: Rabba and Rav Yosef, who both said:
phrases.notes: Attribution line. It introduces the new answer.

phrases.english: Here we are dealing with two sets of witnesses,
phrases.notes: This redefines the case in the משנה.

phrases.english: one says: it became impure while it was still day,
phrases.notes: If true, the עירוב is not valid.

phrases.english: and one says: after nightfall.
phrases.notes: If true, the עירוב is valid, because the food was pure at בין השמשות.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה וְרַב יוֹסֵף דְּאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ הָכָא בִּשְׁתֵּי כִּיתֵּי עֵדִים עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the challenge in Step 15 against רבי ירמיה by offering a different case setup that resolves the contradiction from Steps 12-13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (אוקימתא): the doubt comes from contradictory testimony, not from unknown facts.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The doubt in the משנה looked like the same kind of doubt as the corpse case, so רבי מאיר seemed to contradict himself. רבי ירמיה's attempt to separate the cases left רבי יוסי's ruling hard to explain.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about two sets of witnesses who contradict each other about when the תרומה became impure. That kind of doubt is different from the corpse case.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The doubtful עירוב is a case of two sets of witnesses: one says the תרומה became impure before שבת, and the other says after nightfall.
